en: The Sūtra on the Fruits of the Ascetic Life, spoken by the Buddha, translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Tanwulan of the Western Regions during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Jīyì Mango Grove in the city of Rājagṛha, together with [his assembly].
The Master was accompanied by a multitude of one thousand two hundred and fifty [monks].

At that time, on the fifteenth day of the seventh month, after the conclusion of the New Year’s *kṣayamāsa*, King Ajātaśatru, together with his ministers and officials, surrounded by his retinue, ascended to the Tranquil and Peaceful Observation Hall and addressed his ministers, saying:

"You gentlemen should know that although I have practiced in this way, my untimely grief and distress have not changed; though I have reached this year, I remain in a state of agitation and misery beyond measure."
"What skillful means should be employed to remove his trepidation?
A minister addressed the king:
"One should dispel his anxieties by means of the five kinds of pleasure."
A certain minister said:
"One should employ famous performers, clever and extraordinary entertainers, with drums, music, stringed instruments, and song; these can cure his sorrow.
Another minister addressed the king:
"It would be appropriate to dispel this despondency by deploying the fourfold army—elephants, cavalry, chariots, and brave infantry.
A minister addressed the king:

"The teachers Pūraṇa Kāśyapa, Maskarī Gośālīputra, Ajita Keśakambalin, Kakuda Kātyāyana, Sañjayin Vairaṭīputra, and Nirgrantha Jñātiputra—all these masters reside in this great city, each accompanied by a retinue of five hundred followers."
"You may prepare the imperial carriage and go to meet him; by conversing and listening to his discourse with joy, you may be freed from your affliction.
At that time, there was a physician-king named Jīvaka (in the Jin language, Gùhuó), who was holding a fan and attending upon the king.
The King looked back and said to him,
"Why do you remain silent, alone offering no report?
Jīvaka replied to the King:

"If you wish to dispel burning anxiety, forget your sorrows, and eliminate your afflictions, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, is currently at the Āmra Grove together with his assembly of disciples. You may go to the Buddha’s presence, prostrate yourself to pay your respects, and inquire about your doubts; only then will you attain understanding and liberation."
At that time, King Ajātaśatru, desiring immediately to see the God among Gods, replied to Jīvaka, saying:
"Excellent! Very well;
we shall go together to pay our respects."
Jīvaka received these instructions and prepared five hundred elephants and five hundred court ladies; having finished the preparations, he reported:
"Everything is ready.
May you know that the time has come."
The King mounted his elephant named *Vinīta*, accompanied by five hundred attendants who escorted him before and behind as he departed from Rājagṛha, lighting great torches.
At that time, the king was terrified and halted, unable to proceed, and asked Jīvaka,
"With how many bhikṣus is the Buddha currently staying in the Amra Grove? He replied:
"There are one thousand two hundred and fifty.
The King said,
"I fear you are deceiving me, intending to send me out of the country and endanger me on the way?"
"Whenever I go to the dwellings of the various brahmins of other paths, their assembly numbers five hundred and their voices resound loudly.
Why is it that now there are many bhikṣus, yet no sound is heard? Jīvaka replied:
"O King! Do not fear, do not be anxious.
We dare not plot against Your Majesty, nor do we intend to commit any rebellious harm against the Queen or the nobles."
"Only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, remains tranquil throughout the long night; his disciples are dedicated to their studies, and the Dharma is serene.
May Your Majesty first behold this supreme and wondrous radiance, and see the assembly of the Buddha, the World-Honored One’s disciples; only then will your mind find joy."

Thereupon, King Ajātaśatru saw the World-Honored One from afar and immediately dismounted from his vehicle. He secluded himself from the five sensory pleasures, removed his royal crown, turban, necklaces, precious robes, banners, flowers, and emerald feathers; he set aside his parasol and sheathed his sword.
Walking on foot to the lecture hall, he asked Jīvaka, "Where is the Buddha?"
He replied, "It is the one sitting at the head of the assembly of bhikṣus; his majestic spiritual power is radiant and his merit is sublime.

The king approached the Buddha, exchanged greetings, and withdrew to stand to one side. Observing the Buddha and the assembly of bhikṣus—all seated in tranquil concentration, immeasurably pure, profound, and subtle—he felt great joy in his heart. Joining his palms toward the Buddha, he addressed the World-Honored One:
"The Buddha's mind is tranquil, subtle, and free from thought; his disciples are likewise so.
I pray that my own mind may be resolved upon such subtle and hidden concentration.
A youth named Po Xian addressed the king, saying:
“Great King, do you wish to attain this practice?
The king addressed the Buddha, saying,
“Indeed, World-Honored One!”
"I pray that the assembly of monks may find joy in their hearts.
Thereupon, King Ajātaśatru addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I wish to ask a question; if there be permission to do so, I would venture to speak."
The Buddha said, "Ask whatever you wish. The king said:

"Regarding those things provided for service, as well as various desires, entertainment, sleep, gathering together, deliberation, arithmetic, seals, ministers, the hundred officials and their retinues, the Grand Astrologer who divines omens and knows the beginning and end of a person's life, receiving the respect of others, food and drink, and the arts—whether for oneself, one’s parents, wife and children, or servants;

or in making offerings to śramaṇas and brahmins, giving superior gifts, and seeking the benefits of peace, security, and auspiciousness—is there anyone established in this Buddha’s Dharma and Vinaya who has attained the realization of the Path?"
The Buddha said, "Great King,
have you ever asked such a matter to the various non-Buddhist heterodox teachers?"
The King addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I once went to the place of Pūraṇa Kāśyapa and asked him:

‘Regarding all elephants, horses, chariots, and foot-soldiers; wealth, treasures, and attendants; storehouses; powerful warriors; great elephant-chariots; amusements and sleep; and the assembly of gods and humans—[what is the nature of these things?]’”
The ministers holding seals of office, the hundred officials, and their retinues;
the Grand Historian who divines portents and knows the beginning and end of a person’s life—all these are worthy of reverence.

Whatever they undertake, whether for their own sake to seek peace and security, or for the sake of their parents, wives, children, and servants, they provide offerings to śramaṇas and brahmins, bestowing the highest gifts.
"Could I truly attain the correctness of the Dharma and Vinaya and enter the path of tranquility?
He then replied to me, saying:
"There is no such thing; there is neither a World-Honored One, nor an answer to his great kindness."
Furthermore, there is neither sin nor merit, nor are there parents.
There are no arhats who have attained the Way, and making offerings brings no blessing.
There is neither this world nor the next, nor is there any dedicated practice of the will for the Way through single-mindedness.
Thus, although one possesses a body and life, after the end of one's lifespan, the four elements disperse and perish; the mind ceases and returns to nothingness, never to be born again.
Though buried and interred in the earth, each decays of its own accord until all is exhausted like space, leaving nothing behind.
"So be it, World-Honored One!
I questioned the teachers of external paths, and this was their reply.
Then I thought to myself:"
“Is there not? How can it be that there is no retribution for sin or merit?
It is like a person who, when asked about a *nài* (a plum), answers with a melon; or when asked about a melon, answers with a *nài*.
"Pūraṇa Kāśyapa is also like this; his speech is inverted and lacks coherence from beginning to end. Although I heard what he said, I did not understand it.
King Ajātaśatru addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I also went to the place of Maskarī Gośālīputra and asked him:"
"What is meant by 'the sphere of small desires' and 'the sphere of desire'?
Can a person attain purity without causes and conditions?
Does a person possess transgressions and blessings?"
"Are they without knowledge and without vision?
They also replied to me:
"There is no present world nor a future world; there is neither power nor lack of power, and no spiritual exertion; all people obtain their suffering and pleasure."
"If one asks about six [factors] and answers with seven, World-Honored One!
It is like asking about a mango and answering with a melon, or asking about a melon and answering with a mango; such is the way of these heterodox practitioners."

Within my own country, when they ask what ought to be asked, they are answered accordingly; yet when they ask what they themselves have already said, they are not enlightened or resolved, and thus they immediately depart.
“I further went to the place of Āyupāla and asked:
‘What is meant by the dwelling-place of desire?
How does one attain the realization of the Path within this Dharma and Vinaya?’”
He replied to me, saying: "Yes, Great King!
When others go to ask him, he likewise gives this answer, saying:"
"There is a future life and rebirth.
When I questioned him, he likewise said:
"There is a future life."
"If there is a future life and one is reborn in the world, will it be that there is such a thing or that there is not?
"According to my own understanding, there may be a future life, or there may be no future life."
Suppose someone goes there to ask, saying:
"Is there an afterlife, or is there no afterlife? Is it so, or is it not?
This is like a person who, when asked about a pear, answers with a melon; or when asked about a melon, answers with a pear.
Āḷāra Kālāma was also like this; when I asked him about the realization of the path attained by a śramaṇa and about various matters concerning diverse arts, his answers were incoherent.
I thought to myself:

"None of the heterodox teachers in the entirety of Rājagṛha can provide me with liberation or dispel my sorrow. Where shall I find a śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa who can resolve my thoughts and free me from this distress?"
Seeing that what Āyupāla had said was of no benefit, he rose and departed.
"I then went to Pāṭikāputra and asked:
'What is meant by the place of abiding?'"
I roughly inquired about the origins of the animals and asked,
"According to this system of law and order, how does one attain the Way and realize its fruits?
They answered me, saying:
"O Great King! For those who receive a physical body, there is neither cause nor condition. There is no conceptualization and no arrogance;

yet through the accumulation of harmful acts, they find a place of abiding while remaining established, and thus obtain a body that is never lost. Whatever perceptions they conceive flow forth of their own accord—namely, notions of sin and merit, or good and evil. When a person is severed or struck by what the eyes behold, there is no dispute or contention; when the lifespan of the body ends, they do not grieve over death."
Therein, there is no such thing as saying, "I shall die because of desire," nor is it said that gods and humans speak of the end of life and passing away for the sake of [escaping] desire.
Thus, in the human world, there are the dust and toil of craving; among devas and humans, they perceive desire, and with that desire, there arise the five thieves and sixty-two kinds [of views].

Regarding those sixty-two types [of views]: they are without inherent nature (*gotra*), yet all are said to involve sixty-two matters; when associated with such a nature, conceptualization is useless.
One should abandon all that enters the eight difficult conditions (*aṣṭāvakṣaṇa*); by doing so, one will always attain increase and subsequently achieve peace and security.

Having attained peace and security, one constantly dwells among the devas; once dwelling among the devas, there arise eighty-four great mindfulnesses, which coexist with illusionary arts and coexist with the sublime, yet from them arise the sufferings of old age and sickness.
"There are no practitioners of the Way, nor are there any brahmins.
Such is what has been taught.
My precepts are pure, and I am further detached from craving and desire; having exhausted all desire, it constantly follows my body."
"It is like a lamp that has already been lit; such is the nature of things—that there are no brahmins who have attained the Way.
It is like a person who, when asked about a mango, answers with a melon, and when asked about a melon, answers with a mango.
"Pāṭikāputra was like this: when I questioned the śramaṇa regarding the realization of the Path, he answered me with the words of an old man who is ill.
I thought to myself:
'I asked about the realization of the Path, yet he instead answers with this?'"
Hearing what he said, I was not pleased and did not find it convincing; I then rose and withdrew.
I went again to where Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra was and asked him:
"I ask about the desires in which you dwell."
"In these laws and precepts, how does one achieve the Way?
He answered me, saying: "Yes, Great King!"

Whatever a person has done or is taught to do, whatever they ought to do—whether it be what is to be severed, what is to be taken away, or the seeing that is to be detached from—all that is sought is wearying; thus, sorrow and anxiety are cast off of their own accord.

One may smash jars and blockages, abandon stinginess and greed, destroy cities and towns, and bring ruin and harm to the people; even if one commits acts such as killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, double-tongued speech, drinking alcohol, and inciting strife, there shall be no guilt or calamity.
Regarding that which is given in charity, there is no meritorious retribution.
One who commits violence and rebellion, performing various unwholesome deeds, incurs neither sin nor merit, nor is there anything to be gained from what one does.
"There are no causes or conditions, there is no sincerity, and there is no simplicity.
Even if one practices righteous principles, there will be no response from good or evil.
This is like asking about a pear and answering with a melon, or asking about a melon and answering with a pear.

Pīḷu was also like this; when asked about the practice of the Dharma and whether one would attain the realization of the Path, he answered with further interruptions that there is neither sin nor merit.
I thought to myself:
"Why is this so? Not understanding this, he immediately withdrew and departed.
"I then went again to the place of the Nirgranthas and asked the Nirgranthas:"
"What is meant by 'attaining a place of abode'? Is there anyone in the realm of desire?
What are the offenses and merits one receives?
Are they the result of deeds in previous lives?"
"Is it for the sake of attaining the Way that one studies the Way? He replied to me,
saying, "Yes, Great King!"

Whatever is seen by all people appearing in the present, and whatever offenses or blessings they obtain, are all matters of past lives; they arise from the causal conditions of craving and desire, and through these same causal conditions, there arise old age and sickness.
"In this way, one who studies the Way has the notion of causal conditions; by producing sons and grandsons, one subsequently attains the Way.
This is like asking about a mango and answering with a melon, or asking about a melon and answering with a mango.
"I asked for proof of having attained the Way, yet you answered with false views.
Upon hearing these words, I was neither pleased nor joyful; I immediately rose and withdrew.
King Ajātaśatru addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I have questioned all my teachers, yet I have not attained understanding.
I venture to ask the World-Honored One: where do wealth and treasures reside?
I pray that you will answer my doubts according to what I have asked.”
"How does a śramaṇa or a brāhmaṇa, within this Dharma and Vinaya, attain the realization of the Path?
The Buddha said to the king:
"Ask whatever you wish; I shall explain each matter for you in detail so that the knots of your mind may be untied."
I previously questioned the King, and the King answered with his own intention.
What do you think, Great King?
Suppose there is a person who dresses in fine garments and serves the King for his own pleasure; yet that person does not delight in his dwelling or his native land, and thinks to himself:
"King Ajātaśatru is a human being, and I too am a human being.
The King delights himself with the five sensory pleasures and adorns himself with fine clothing; yet he finds no joy in his native land and harbors no attachment to his dwelling place."

"I shall establish virtue and distance myself from all sinful calamities; it would be better for me to shave my hair and beard, don the kāṣāya, become a śramaṇa, and, with the faith of a householder, leave home to follow the Way."

He then received the Dharma-precepts and reverently practiced the prohibitions of the Path: he did not kill, steal, or engage in sexual misconduct; he did not speak falsely, use double-tongued speech, or utter harsh words and abuse; and he was free from anger, envy, and delusion.
"What do you think, O King? Suppose a person who attends upon Your Majesty with fine adornments were to say:

'I take no pleasure in my dwelling, nor do I harbor attachment to my homeland; with the faith of a householder, I have left home for the path of the Way. I guard my body, speech, and mind, refrain from all evils, and practice the ten wholesome deeds.'"
"What can the King do about this?
The King said to the Buddha:

"When I see such a person, I shall joyfully greet them, respectfully offer salutations and veneration, and provide offerings of clothing, food and drink, bedding and furniture, and medicine for the sick."
The Buddha said to the king:
"That person has not yet practiced the Great Dharma, yet they have attained the realization of the fruits of the Path.
The king addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Take up his teaching of the Dharma.
The Buddha said to the king:

"I am, for the world, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the One Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, the Sugata, the Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed One, the Tamer of Men, the Teacher of Gods and Humans, called the Buddha, the World-Honored One."

He then preached the Dharma, which was excellent in its beginning, excellent in its middle, and excellent in its conclusion; it was perfectly endowed with profound meaning and wisdom, expounding upon pure conduct.
If an elder has a son who hears the sutras preached by the Buddha, gains faith in the Tathāgata’s Dharma and Vinaya, and perceives his own well-being;
and if, within the Buddha's teachings, he realizes there is great and sublime benefit and immediately attains the patience of the Dharma (dharmakṣānti), remaining settled in every thought-moment.
Living at home is constrained by defilements;
those who have left the home life are free from such hindrances. Thus, they unify their minds to cease and eliminate sensual desires, and for as long as they live, they uphold pure conduct, thinking:

"I wish to abandon my household wealth, family, and kin; I shall shave off my hair and beard, don the kāṣāya robe, and with the faith of a householder, go forth to follow the Way. I shall renounce what is pleasurable to establish the resolve of a renunciant, and I shall observe the two hundred and fifty bhikṣu precepts, not violating the prohibitions of the Path."

One protects the Dharma for crossing over to liberation; in conduct and demeanor, one maintains propriety and does not lose restraint. Suddenly casting aside all possessions, one remains serene, respectful, and cautious.
With single-minded equanimity, one cultivates right precepts: staying far removed from killing, not grasping at swords or staves, and harboring a sense of shame and remorse.
They bring peace to all and do not inflict fear;
their minds are pure, and they harbor no intent to harm.

They stay far removed from theft, abandoning taking what is not given; they delight in giving and are inclined toward renunciation, their thoughts resting in tranquility as they constantly guard themselves.
His mind is pure; he neither gives nor takes.
He stays far removed from sexual conduct, purely cultivating the holy life (*brahmacarya*), intent upon chastity, and extinguishing turbid desires.
His mind is pure; he is not deluded by forms.
He stays far removed from false speech and does not prize empty exaggeration; he never practices deception or guile, but keeps his will fixed on sincerity and faith.

Abiding in tranquility and certainty, he does not violate his worldly vows. His mind is pure, harboring no deceit or hypocrisy; he takes no pleasure in double-tongued talk that slanders others and ruins virtue. He never spreads rumors to incite strife between this person and that, but instead reconciles disputes and dispels resentment and harm.

With a pure mind, he does not harbor malice toward those who speak divisively; he stays far away from harsh speech and does not delight in reviling others. Always exercising self-restraint, he never indulges in the utterance of unwholesome words. What he says is gentle and compliant, free from coarse or violent expressions; those who hear him are moved to joy and take refuge in him with devotion.

His mind is pure; he never utters abuse, stays far removed from frivolous speech, and speaks with measured propriety. He causes no harm, remains grounded in the principles of righteousness and Dharma, and his discourse is composed, tranquil, faultless, and discerning of both principle and circumstance.

His mind is pure; his resolve is free from frivolous speech; he stays far removed from dullness and eliminates ignorance; he does not covet the possessions of others nor seek out the faults of men; regarding both himself and others, he constantly seeks great tranquility.

His mind is pure, free from folly, and far removed from anger; he harbors no intent to harm or injure, but always maintains a heart of loving-kindness. His resolve is fixed upon skillful means, and out of compassion he protects even the crawling insects, feeling shame before all beings and offering them consolation.

His mind was pure, free from resentment and anger; he remained far removed from drowsiness and cultivated the practice of emptiness. He constantly maintained tranquility and never slept soundly, desiring to contemplate the light and wishing to attain awakening.
His mind is pure, his will is free from sleepiness, and he remains far removed from frivolous play, derisive talk, and idle chatter. His conduct is without attachment and devoid of sudden violence.
His mind is pure, his will is not playful, he is far removed from doubt and hesitation, and with a resolute intention, he abides in wholesome dharmas.

His mind is pure and his resolve is free from doubt; he remains far removed from false views. He believes that in this life and in future lives, practicing generosity brings merit; he is filial toward his parents and reveres the worthy and holy; he follows and cultivates the path of goodness, and trusts in the truth that after this life one shall be reborn, attaining the Way, the six supernormal powers, and the practice of equanimity.

Their minds are pure and free from false views; they are far removed from flattery and deceit, and their hearts are simple and honest, harboring no artifice or hypocrisy. They do not use weights, measures, or dimensions to deceive or exploit others; they do not practice binding or imprisonment; being without malice or expectation, they seek only to attain clarity.

His mind is pure, his resolve free from flattery and deceit; he stays far removed from men and women, takes no pleasure in the household life or the desires of wife and children, and eliminates all petty doubts.
His mind is pure, free from worldly ambition; he does not keep slaves, clients, servants, or concubines, nor does he delight in managing a household.
His mind is pure; he does not falsely grasp at things, nor does he keep elephants, horses, oxen, sheep, or cattle, nor does he delight in keeping beasts.
His mind is pure; he does not set his heart on vehicles, nor does he keep chickens, ducks, dogs, or pigs, having no desire for profit or gain.

His mind is pure; he does not concern himself with poultry or pigs, stays far removed from lodgings and mansions, does not decorate his dwellings, and does not maintain fields, houses, gardens, orchards, or fruit-bearing vines.
His mind is pure; he does not dwell in rural estates, stays far away from gold, silver, and high or broad seats, and takes no pleasure in elegant carpets, mats, or tables.
His mind is pure; he does not sleep on high beds, stays far away from the seven treasures, does not keep rare jewels, abandons all playthings, and harbors no hope for worldly glory.
Their minds are pure; they do not covet wealth or beauty, remain far removed from floral fragrances, take no pleasure in mixed scents, their bodies are not perfumed, and they harbor no expectations.
With a pure mind, he has no desire for the fragrance of flowers; he stays far removed from eating at improper times, always observing moderation by taking only one meal a day as his lifelong rule.

With a pure mind, he does not miss the proper time for meals. When plowing the earth to sow seeds, he adorns the interval between them to observe his conduct; he performs the duties of a śramaṇa, purifying his mind, illuminating it against sorrow, and eliminating all defilements and harms. Always practicing what is true and correct, with restraint and contentment, with a single mind fixed on the Path, he then becomes a śramaṇa or brahmacārin, receiving food offered in faith.

Throughout the lands, provinces, districts, and towns, his conduct is in accordance with the Dharma; its root is eternally pure, and its trunk, nodes, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits are likewise pure. It is endowed with all manner of purity, and such is the nature of its manifestation.
In the commanderies, kingdoms, districts, and towns, one acts as a śramaṇa by remaining far removed from these [faults].

If there are śramaṇas or brahmins who ought to consume the offerings of the faithful, they should, wherever they dwell, mindfully contemplate those people and act always in accordance with what is appropriate.

“If there are śramaṇas or brahmins who, wherever they receive food offered out of faith, dwell in places where their conduct is improper; who seek out meals by calculating and scheming; who seek out incense, flowers, robes, bedding, and seats; who hide away precious treasures and seek out such locations—śramaṇas and practitioners of the Way should all keep far away from these.”

If there are śramaṇas or brahmins who, while consuming the food offered out of faith, sit upon high and wide couches, occupy jeweled beds, and pursue their conduct with such things as decorated seats, variegated rugs, embroidered coverlets, fine silks, or fabrics so exquisite that they cause one’s hair to stand on end; if they carry banners and fly-whisks, ride on elephants, carriages, or horses, and seek out choice foods, remaining constantly attached to name-and-form—śramaṇas and practitioners of the Way should all remain far removed from these.

If there are śramaṇas or brahmins who, while consuming the food offered out of faith, bathe at will, act inappropriately, and have abandoned their proper conduct; who perfume themselves with incense and flowers, seek offerings by improper means, carry swords and parasols in their hands, adorn themselves with necklaces and strings of pearls on their arms, wrists, necks, and feet, wear pure white garments, and shorten trees—such is their way of dwelling and acting;
a śramaṇa or practitioner of the Way should keep far away from them.

"If there are śramaṇas or brahmins who, having accepted food offered in faith, adorn their bodies and dwell in places where their conduct is improper—such as watching fights of elephants, oxen, horses, chickens, sheep, dogs, and pigs; inciting strife among men and women, both great and small; or attending battles and large public assemblies—and if they seek to dwell in such ways, then a śramaṇa practitioner should remain far removed from such things."

If there are śramaṇas or brahmins who, having accepted food offered in faith, adorn their bodies with what is improper for them to dwell in and whose conduct is inconsistent with their practice—merely listening to the sounds of elephants, horses, chariots, and people walking, or to the beating of drums, music, song, dance, and playful conversation—such practices belong to heterodox paths;
the śramaṇa practitioner has already distanced himself from these.

If there are śramaṇas or brahmins who, while receiving the food offered in faith by others, engage in games of dice and gambling, dwelling in what is not the Dharma and whose conduct is inconsistent—such as competing and quarreling over *kaṇa*, *kula*, *tumba*, *kharaka*, *kuṇḍa*, *sela*, *thula*, and *luka*—their conduct is such that they dwell in what is not the Dharma;
the śramaṇas and practitioners of the Way have already distanced themselves from this.

If there are śramaṇas or brahmins who, while receiving food offered in faith, constantly engage in quarreling, strife, and contentious speech; whose conduct is unrighteous and whose abiding is unrighteous; and whose behavior is improper, saying:
"This is the Dharma, this is not the Dharma; it is not thus; this is the one true Dharma, and it is not as you say."
"The Dharma I practice is what you ought not to do; that which I do is what you ought to do.
You possess the causal conditions [for rebirth], whereas I have no such conditions.

You went forward yourself and later spoke falsely; I have emerged victorious over you. You have planted nothing but committed manifold evils, so you shall encounter harm and peril; I have attained liberation, while you are cast aside and deprived of autonomy."
"Such are the words of contention and unlawful speech;
the śramaṇa practitioner has already distanced himself from these.
If there are śramaṇas or brahmins who, having consumed the food offered out of faith, engage in idle chatter together, their conduct is improper."
"What is meant by 'kings'?
What is meant by 'thieves'?
What is meant by 'battles'?"
"What is meant by food and drink?
What are clothes, men and women, the large and the small?
To speak of such worldly matters, of causes and effects, of pleasant things—such as these are words that are not the Dharma; the śramaṇa practitioner has already distanced himself from them.

When śramaṇas and brahmins accept food offered in faith, they falsely speak of improper matters; their conduct is inconsistent with their words as they discourse on the affairs of kings and brahmins, the affairs of trees and humans, and the affairs of states—saying, "In this place it shall be thus," "In that country such things will occur," "This person shall go there," or "That person shall come here. Such statements are not in accordance with the Dharma;
the śramaṇa practitioner has already distanced himself from these.

“Śramaṇas and brahmins who, having received food offered out of faith, practice flattery and deceit, act contrary to the Dharma, and engage in improper conduct while sitting together in conversation—thinking ‘this will bring profit’ or ‘this will lead to ruin’—engage in such unrighteous acts of flattery like those who live by trade and commerce.
Śramaṇas and practitioners of the Way have already distanced themselves from these.”

When śramaṇas and brahmins accept food offered out of faith, yet study and practice illusory arts, give rise to false views, speak of solar portents, engage in fortune-telling and the observation of signs, utter falsehoods to seize property, or study various arts and incantations—such as the *kāṇḍarīka* spells, the *māyūra* (peacock) spells, and miscellaneous fragmentary incantations—these are heterodox arts used for deception and delusion;
such practices are unrighteous arts from which the śramaṇa practitioner has already distanced himself.

There are śramaṇas and brahmins who, while receiving food offered in faith, study delusive spells and deceptive arts; they observe facial expressions, the movements of stars, portents, wind, clouds, thunder, and mist; they seek auspicious days and inquire whether it will rain or not in a certain village during the summer months, whether a particular location will be favorable or unfavorable, and they discourse on the affairs of kings—such practices are unlawful arts, from which the śramaṇa practitioner has already distanced himself.

Śramaṇas and brahmins who accept food offered in faith may practice various kinds of improper methods and the occupations of animals: prescribing medicines according to the region, dwelling wherever they please, causing people to become short of breath, to vomit, to purge, or to weep; agitating the blood vessels of others; being insincere and dishonest in intent; and teaching deceptive arts or practicing divination for matters of safety.
Such as these are the occupations of animals; the śramaṇa practitioner has already distanced himself from them.

When śramaṇas and brahmins accept food offered in faith, yet their conduct is contrary to the Dharma, they speak of marriage and betrothal—such as describing those who reside in certain lodgings, in certain halls, or are pregnant in certain chambers; or describing those who dwell in pleasure chambers, or possess palaces for the practice of ascetic vigor, or possess halls and pavilions where there is no such practice—and they speak of various matters concerning kings;
such things as these are the occupations of beasts, from which the śramaṇa practitioner has already distanced himself.

“Śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who accept food offered out of faith yet engage in various kinds of animal-like conduct and the karma of wrong views—such as divining omens from jewels, pearls, oxen, horses, dwellings, and blades; or interpreting the physical marks of men, women, and children of all ages—these are the manifestations of the karma of wrong views.
Śramaṇas and practitioners have already distanced themselves from such things.”

Śramaṇas and brahmins who accept food offered out of faith may have the fundamental conduct of sorcery and delusion, performing unlawful deeds and ignorant acts while considering themselves wise; they practice divination, cast spells, and recite incantations—such as these are the karmic activities of wrong views, from which śramaṇa practitioners have already distanced themselves.

When śramaṇas and brahmins receive food offered out of faith, they may see good omens or bad omens, and then pre-emptively declare that grain will become scarce and expensive or that it will be plentiful and cheap; they predict there will be terror or tranquility, or that there will be a great pestilence and death. Such things as these are the karmic results of wrong views;
the śramaṇa practitioners have already distanced themselves from them.

When śramaṇas and brahmins, having accepted food offered out of faith, declare that a certain king will be victorious in battle while another king shall not prevail; or that a certain king will go on an excursion to observe another country while the ruler of that other country will lose his sovereignty; or that this one shall be victorious while that one shall be defeated; or that this king possesses many elephants, horses, livestock, and chariots while that king has few elephants, horses, and chariots—such as these are the karmic results of wrong views.
Śramaṇas and practitioners have already distanced themselves from such things.

When śramaṇas and brahmins accept food offered in faith, they may discuss the regular movement of the sun and moon, their deviations; the regular movement of the stars and constellations, their deviations; the irregularities in the speed of the sun and moon’s revolutions; impending calamities and extraordinary changes; solar and lunar eclipses; or rain, frost, hail, and thunderbolts—such as these are the karmic results of false views;
but the śramaṇa practitioner has already distanced himself from these.

When śramaṇas and brahmins, having accepted food offered in faith, proclaim that the sun and moon move in their proper courses, or that they move contrary to their courses; that the stars have causes and conditions for their proper movements and also causes and conditions for their contrary movements; that there are obstructions and portents; that the sun and moon travel westward, or some say they travel eastward; or that an eclipse will occur, while others say it will not; or that there will be thunder, lightning, and thunderbolts—such phenomena they claim to constantly witness and verify.
Yet, the śramaṇa practitioners who have already distanced themselves from these things are called noble sages.

"My disciples, the śramaṇas, uphold these precepts of the noble ones and practice knowing contentment: they take clothing only to cover their bodies and food only to fill their mouths; wherever they travel, their robes and bowls accompany them, and they have no lingering attachment to anything."
Just as a bird flying through the air has its two wings following its body,
so it is with a bhikṣu who upholds the noble precepts, whose mind knows contentment, and who harbors no expectations.
Once he had mastered the rules of deportment, his movements were secure and peaceful, and his conduct was entirely composed and dignified.
Whether looking straight ahead or glancing around, he never lost his proper decorum.
In his bending and stretching, advancing and retreating, he acted according to the Dharma and what was appropriate; his sitting and rising were calm and elegant, and his conduct remained unimpaired.

Upholding this chapter on precepts, one is foremost in contentment; the gates of the senses are tranquil and stilled, and the mind dwells in the state of peace. The faculties are not distracted, and one guards the mind, rescuing it so that it remains free from conceptualization while on the path. When the eyes behold beautiful forms, one does not conceive of them with desire or regard them as beautiful, but cuts off all that is received.
Practicing the roots of goodness, his mind dwells within, remaining detached from internal forms while guarding the faculty of the eye.
Likewise, regarding sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles of the ear, nose, tongue, and body, he does not seek them through conceptualization, nor does he have any attachment to them.

Eliminating all that is improper, abandoning the treatment of folly, and severing unwholesome dharmas, he causes the mind to dwell within, rescuing it from distraction and bringing the faculties of the mind to concentration.

That bhikṣu upholds these noble and holy precepts, possessing supreme contentment; his mind is tranquil and settled, his sense faculties are disciplined through ritual decorum, and he remains unaroused within. He moves with ease and security, dwelling in quietude and seclusion—among mountains and thickets, avoiding vulgarity, in rocky caves and wilderness retreats. With his body at rest therein, he is detached from the world and free from cleverness, his mind contemplating the state of non-conceptualization.
They do not covet the possessions of others, do not give rise to delusion, and do not intrude upon or disturb others.
They constantly practice a mind of loving-kindness; their intentions are pure, and they are free from thoughts of ignorance.
Wandering wherever he goes, his mind is free from attachment; he is joyful, virtuous, peaceful, and secure.

It is like a person traveling far away to seek profit who passes through a perilous road and succeeds in crossing the narrow defiles; having acquired great profit and lost nothing, he provides for his wife, children, and kinsmen, and thinks to himself:
"My heart is filled with great joy."
"In this way, monks, one remains far removed from delusion; the mind is pure and free from defilement; having eliminated malice and harm, it is joyful and unsullied."

It is like a person who falls ill and is confined to bed, remaining weak and exhausted for many years. Later, he recovers and becomes peaceful, secure, and strong; his food is properly digested, and he thinks to himself:
"I was once in a state of extreme distress, but now I have been cured."
"In this way, a bhikṣu eliminates a mind of anger; through mature self-reflection, his mind becomes joyful.

It is like a person who serves as another's subordinate, bound by fetters and subjected to labor without end, never finding leisure or autonomy. Later, having escaped and become a free commoner, he thinks to himself:
'I was formerly a slave to others, but now I have been liberated,' and his heart leaps with joy."
The bhikṣu, having cast away doubt and being free from hesitation, stands established in purity, filled with joy and exultation.
It is like a person who has been imprisoned in a dungeon, suffering the bitterness of torture, and then finally escapes; he thinks to himself:
"I was once confined in darkness, but now I have attained liberation; how fortunate I am!"
"In this way, the bhikṣu eliminates doubt; his mind becomes pure and flawless, filled with joy. The bhikṣu removes the improper mind; with a correct mind free from blemish, he purifies his resolve."

For example, suppose there is a person who encounters a time of high grain prices and is terrified by the threat of famine; having obtained relief and security, their life is preserved, and they find themselves amidst abundance when grain becomes plentiful and cheap. Living in leisure and without fear, they think to themselves:
"I was formerly destitute and hungry, in a state of peril beyond description; now I have attained fullness and peace, and my heart is filled with joy."

"In this way, the bhikṣu eliminates improper thoughts and is free from manifold perceptions and mental formations. Having set aside his original state of purity and being without doubt, he removes the five hindrances; through the power of his mind, he distances himself from worldly toil and attains wisdom. Thus he is liberated from all calamities, having cast off imprisonment, hunger, and all unwholesome states of craving. Possessing perception and mental formations, he dwells in tranquility and purity, practicing the first dhyāna."
It is as if a person enters the water to bathe; once cleansed and free from defilement, they step onto the bank with a joyful heart. So it is with the bhikṣu:

dwelling alone in stillness, tranquil and delighted, he contemplates the body’s original arising; seeing that no body exists, he universally observes that there are no roots. His mental activity is stilled, and he is joyful, peaceful, and established in the foremost state of single-minded concentration.

By means of this concentration, his mind becomes pure and he abides in tranquility; attaining non-differentiation, with craving exhausted and perceptions and formations removed, he is inwardly fulfilled in mindfulness, dwelling in peace and performing wholesome deeds—this is the second state of single-mindedness.

Furthermore, with this very body, one attains samādhi; joyful and at ease, being without obstruction, one possesses complete vision. Being without any class of physical form and having achieved that which is beyond comparison, one shall be settled in joy.

For example, it is like the blue lotus, the water lily, and the fragrant *henghua*, which grow from muddy sludge and are nurtured within the water; although they are in the water, their roots, leaves, flowers, and fruits remain unattached to the water and are not defiled by it.
In this way, the bhikṣu, with this body and through samādhi, dwells in peace and joy.

By means of this mind of right attainment, he reaches firm stability and attains non-differentiation; he purifies his mind so that it is free from the dust of desire—this is the third single-mindedness.

With this mind, his body is at peace and his mind is settled in tranquil composure and non-attachment; even if there were no body, he would universally contemplate its total non-existence, neither feeling further joy nor agitation, but remaining peaceful and undisturbed.
It is like a mountain that is solid and complete without defect, vast and boundless; when wind comes from the east, it cannot move it, and the same is true for winds from the south, west, and north.
Why is this? Because their lower roots are firm and cannot be shaken.

Within it flows water that is cool and delicious, incapable of being defiled; for it relies upon the mountain, flowing in full abundance and spreading everywhere, reaching all places because the water is pure.

In this way, a bhikṣu contemplates the body; finding nothing therein to delight in, he rests in security, his practice being complete. Contemplating until no self-body remains, he then perceives universally.

By means of this state of mind, he practices with tranquility; it is pure and stainless, firmly established and unwavering. Having eliminated craving and desire, he dwells in the fourth dhyāna with one-pointed mind, where there is neither suffering nor pleasure, but equanimity.

It is, for example, like a person on the seventh or eighth day of the month who puts on new clothes, with a joyful countenance, looking about to ensure there is no one naked, desiring to wear these excellent and wonderful garments.

In this way, a bhikṣu’s bodily conduct is pure and his mind is stainless; he attains liberation with joy, acting without a fixed abode and perceiving no self-body. He universally contemplates the absence of location, employing a pure mind free from all defilements.

For example, suppose there were a great lecture hall not far from a commandery, a kingdom, a district, or a town. A person atop it kindled a fire and produced light; that light shone equally, neither high nor low. The wind could not extinguish it, birds could not cover it, and no other species could obscure the light; it remained firm, stable, and unmoving.

In this way, the bhikṣu’s mind is undisturbed, remaining firm and unshakable; having attained emptiness and purity, the bhikṣu understands thus: "I have attained right concentration, and my body is tranquil."

This body composed of the four great elements is born of father and mother and serves as the support for the soul and spirit; yet one finds no joy in discarding this body. One should constantly establish the body and mind so as to find weariness and revulsion toward them, never again to undergo rebirth. This causes the mind to be without form, eliminating all categories of physical existence and the various seeds of the body, while not losing the foundation upon which the body and mind are established. Thus, one manifests various bodies, fully endowed with all marks of excellence, without any deficiency.
It is like pulling up the roots and stumps of grass and trees; one who sees clearly knows that once the root is pulled out, they will not grow again.

In this same way, a bhikṣu understands this: he perceives that whatever belongs to his body is composed of name-and-form (nāmarūpa), a synthesis of the four great elements (mahābhūta), born of father and mother, nourished by food and clothing, and shrouded in falsehood. What solidity is there in it?
It is a dharma that extinguishes through friction, the basis upon which the soul and spirit rely; it causes them to abide without confusion and remain unshakable.

I shall establish my body and mind, manifesting various bodies; though they are devoid of physical form or mind, they are fully endowed with appearance, their faculties unimpaired. Arising from samādhi, I manifest numerous bodies, each complete in its appearance.
It is, for example, like a person who takes a viper out of a basket; a wise person seeing it knows it to be a basket containing four serpents. So it is with the bhikṣu:

clearly understanding this, he realizes that this physical body is sustained by warmth, a composite of the four great elements, born of father and mother, upon which the soul-spirit relies. He establishes his mind and body, manifesting various forms; though devoid of name-and-form, it is fully endowed with physical appearance and its faculties are unimpaired. Rising from samādhi, he transforms himself into countless bodies.
It is, for example, as when someone draws a sword from its scabbard; one who is discerning sees that there is a sharp iron blade within the scabbard, now drawn forth.
In this same way, a bhikṣu who understands this thoroughly observes that person, manifesting countless forms, complete with all marks of excellence, without any deficiency.

“By means of this samādhi-attainment, the bhikṣu’s mind is pure, free from blemish, and cleansed of worldly toil; it is supple and desireless, firmly established and immovable. Having attained the wisdom of the divine feet and the wisdom of the superknowledges (abhijñā), his mind neither increases nor decreases; his conduct is equanimous, and he is noble, sovereign, and fearless in thought.”

He transforms a single body into countless bodies, and causes those countless bodies to return to being one; he manifests transformations alone, and with manifold wisdom, he passes through walls without any trace of obstruction.

For example, it is like a flying bird roaming through space, emerging from the uninterrupted and entering the poreless; it enters the earth without obstruction, as if entering water or walking upon the surface of water.

For example, as if walking upon the earth while remaining in mid-air, he sits in the full lotus posture like a bird amidst the clouds; there, he grasps and strokes with his hand the sun and moon in all their vast majesty and power, and transforms his body to ascend as far as the ninth Brahma-heaven.
Just as a skillful and clever potter, having prepared his clay and taken a good mold, shapes it into vessels so that nothing he makes fails to succeed;
even so, a bhikṣu who has attained supernormal powers can manifest transformations at will, reaching as far as the Brahma Heaven.
Just as a trainer of elephants or horses trains various elephants and horses until they all achieve mastery, so it is with the bhikṣu:
through supernormal powers and transformations, his body reaches the Brahma Heaven.
Just as a skilled goldsmith, through his craftsmanship, takes purple-gold and fashions armlets, necklaces, seals, and radiant ornaments, accomplishing them all according to his will;
so too is the bhikṣu, through his supernormal powers and transformations, able to extend his body as far as the Brahma-heaven.

The bhikṣu maintains the meditative absorption of samādhi; his mind is pure and without blemish, reaching the realization of wisdom and attaining supernormal powers. His mind is free from attachment, his eye can see through, perceiving the destinies of good and evil among the heavens above and the world below; his ear can hear through, hearing the speech of devas and humans, as well as the sounds of crawling insects, breathing creatures, and all beings.
It is like a wise man who, standing upon a high platform, blows a great sounding horn with all his might, and its sound is heard in all four directions.

In the same way, the bhikṣu possesses the divine ear (*divya-śrotra*) that hears clearly; he hears and knows all the destinies of gods and humans, whether good or evil. Having attained the supernormal power (*abhijñā*) of realization through the Path, he universally and thoroughly knows the thoughts in the minds of others—whether they are wholesome or unwholesome, full of desire or free from desire, full of anger or free from anger, full of compassion or devoid of compassion, full of delusion or free from delusion, possessed of discernment or lacking discernment, burdened by afflictions or free from afflictions, having attained realization of the Path or not having attained it, whether their minds are distracted or tranquil, whether they are diligent or indolent, and whether their merit and wisdom are limited or limitless—he knows them all.

It is like a district, state, or town where, not far away, there is a large pavilion or a high tower; a person dwelling upon it sees countless people coming and going, entering and exiting. A wise person, seeing this, observes those who enter and exit.
"In this way, the bhikṣu perceives the good and evil, the right and wrong, within the minds of others, extending universally to all forms and species throughout the world.
The Buddha said:

"That bhikṣu who has attained supernormal powers recollects the events of incalculable past ages; with a mind of wisdom or a mind of delusion, he sees one lifetime, ten lifetimes, a hundred lifetimes, a thousand lifetimes, ten thousand lifetimes, a hundred thousand lifetimes, and countless lifetimes—wandering and revolving through them, witnessing the formation and destruction of heaven and earth."

He fully knows the past lives of these beings: from where they came to be born here; the names of the lands where they resided; their caste, family name, and physical appearance; their height, whether they were handsome or ugly, or good or evil; how they passed away from there to be born here, and how they pass away from here to be born there.

For example, suppose there is a person who goes from this village to another village; while there, they sit, stand, speak, lie down, sleep, and remain silent. Then, returning from that village back to this one, they sit, stand, speak, and walk about—all of these actions are clearly perceived and recognized.
"In this way, a bhikṣu’s consciousness is like the ocean; he perceives the countless events of the past.

The Buddha said, "A bhikṣu who has attained supernormal powers possesses a mind that is pure and transparent; his eye of the Way sees through all things, surpassing the fundamental nature of ordinary men."
One observes people being born into existence—whether good or evil, beautiful or ugly—and their return to either the path of goodness or the path of evil.

If a person’s body performs good deeds, their speech utters good words, and their mind conceives good thoughts, they maintain right contemplation and are free from false views; based on this foundation, at the end of their life, they attain rebirth in the heavens.

If a person’s body performs evil deeds, their speech utters evil words, and their mind conceives evil thoughts, based on this foundation, after the death of the body, they fall into the paths of evil.
For example, it is like a person standing atop a high tower who watches people coming and going, entering and exiting, sitting, rejoicing, or grieving.
In this same way, a bhikṣu who has attained supernormal powers and possesses the eye of the Path—penetrating, pure, and without blemish—beholds the events of the past and the future.
The Buddha said:
"A bhikṣu who has attained supernormal powers, whose outflows are exhausted, and who has realized the three types of higher knowledge through wisdom, does not harbor frivolous doubts.

He understands the truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path; he eliminates the outflows and becomes free from them, devoid of deluded thoughts, seeing their very root with profound and unerring clarity."

Having seen and known thus, he has crossed over the outflow of sensual desire; as for the outflow of ignorance, his mind is pure and liberated. Being thus liberated, he is endowed with the knowledge of having crossed over; birth and death are severed, the holy life has been attained, what was to be done has been accomplished, and he knows the root of name-and-form.
The Buddha said:
"Great King! These are the fruits of the path of the śramaṇa in the present."
Thereupon, King Ajātaśatru of Magadha rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and confessed his transgression:
“I only pray that the World-Honored One will forgive my offenses.”
For example, it is like a child who is foolish and lacks wisdom, who is deluded and loses his resolve, and possesses no skillful means.
The Buddha is the King of Dharma and the parent of all; he constantly establishes the True Dharma, rescuing the deluded by instituting the Law, free from anger, harm, and the hindrances.
If I may be born anew now, I pray that the World-Honored One will accept my prostration and take refuge in you.
Having recognized my own transgressions and evils, I shall further receive your instructions and admonitions; I will punish and reform my past ways and cultivate myself in accordance with the future.
The Buddha said, "Great King! As you have said,
he was indeed like a child— foolish and lacking wisdom, deluded and devoid of skillful means, who took the lives of his own parents."
Now that I have taken refuge in the Dharma King, I have attained rebirth; I personally recognize my transgressions.
Within this system of Dharma and Vinaya, I have gained wholesome benefit and shall suffer no loss.
Then King Ajātaśatru joined his palms toward the Buddha and said,
“I only pray that the World-Honored One, together with the assembly of bhikṣus, will accept my offerings.
At that time, the Buddha accepted the invitation by remaining silent.
Knowing that his invitation had been accepted, the king’s heart leaped with joy; he circumambulated the Buddha three times, prostrated himself, and withdrew.
Once the king had retired, not far from the Buddha, he addressed the youth Jīvaka:

“You have brought me great benefit, for you have led me to the Buddha to receive his dharma instructions. Having been able to behold the World-Honored One, my transgressions have been absolved, and my heavy guilt has been lightened.”
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"King Ajātaśatru has already attained patience toward living beings (sattvakṣānti).

Although he harmed the Dharma King, he has completely eliminated his defilements; being free from all outflows (āsrava), he abides in the Dharma without wavering. While seated here, he has distanced himself from dust and left behind defilement, and the Dharma-eye has arisen."

The king returned to his palace and that very night prepared a hundred kinds of exquisite meals and delicacies. At dawn, he went to the Buddha’s dwelling, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and said to him:
“The time has come; we pray that the World-Honored One will deign to grace us with his presence.”
The Buddha, together with the community of bhikṣus and surrounded by his retinue, proceeded to the royal palace.
Once the Buddha and the assembly were seated, the water for washing was served; then food was laid out, and the King personally served them until they had finished eating and rinsing their mouths.
The king took a small couch and sat before the Buddha to listen to him preach the sutra.
The king addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Indeed, World-Honored One, I pray that you will accept my invitation for one summer retreat."

In the royal palace, he provided whatever was lacking as offerings; furthermore, for the sake of the Buddha and the assembly of bhikṣus, he established five hundred vihāras, so that the one thousand two hundred and fifty [monks] would have places to rest and sleep.
"The rice and grain in the storehouses, whether for the inner palace or for those of high or low rank, should be offered as provisions.
The Buddha said, "Great King, if you are joyful, then your offerings will be complete; however, I have already accepted the invitation from the elder Sudatta of Śrāvastī for one summer retreat."
The king addressed the Buddha, saying, “That elder of the kingdom has gained a sublime benefit, for the Buddha, the God among Gods, first accepted his invitation.
At that time, the Buddha preached the Dharma for King Ajātaśatru, causing his mind to open and be liberated; the Buddha then spoke these verses:
"Those who perform fire sacrifices all consider themselves supreme;
the king is the most honored among men; the ocean is the source of all streams;
among the constellations, the moon is bright; and the sun sheds its light during the day."
"Throughout the realms above and below where beings come and go, among all classes of sentient beings, and across the heavens and the world, the Buddha-way is the most honored.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, King Ajātaśatru, the assembly of bhikṣus, and the devas and asuras rejoiced upon hearing the sutra; they paid homage and departed.
The Sūtra on the Fruits of the Ascetic Life Spoken by the Buddha
